name: Jade Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm out of the Eastside depot by half six, and our crew is four of us on one bucket truck, with Dev as foreman. Most days it's overhead distribution work in the city: swapping a rotten pole, re-sagging a line a lorry clipped, replacing a cooked transformer behind somebody's garden. I like the problem in front of you and the way the crew talks without talking, a nod means hold it, a hand flat means stop.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Storm call-outs, mostly. Last February I did three nights of eighteen hours, and you come home with your hands shaking from the cold and the kids already off to school. And the paperwork they keep adding. They gave us a tablet app last year that wants photos of everything, and I still write my notes in a pocket book first, because I trust my own pencil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At the union meeting I'd be the one saying all that money went into chatbots while our crews are still short two people per depot. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it'd be a relief. My work stays my work, my pay keeps going up with the contract, and the mortgage on our place on Harrow Road gets paid on time. I'd just be glad nobody makes me talk to a computer to log a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes much. I'd keep putting a bit aside every month like we already do, we've got about ten months of bills in the savings account. I'd keep going to branch meetings, and I'd keep refusing the AI report thing for as long as they let me fill in the paper form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest. Like when everyone panics about a storm and it blows out to sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned refusing the AI report tool. What happens when they stop allowing the paper form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'll use it, grumbling. Dev already types up half my notes for me because he knows I won't. I'm not proud of that, but I'd rather spend my energy up the pole than poking at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, who comes out ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same people who always do. The company's shareholders get a nice story for a year and a few office jobs get trimmed. The crews stay where we are, which is fine, because our contract is decent. We fought for that.

S0.say: I'd tell the union branch it was hype all along, and that the money spent on chatbots should have gone on hiring the two lineworkers each depot is short.
S0.think: Privately I'd be relieved, because my job, my rising pay and our mortgage would all carry on as they are. Nobody would make me talk to a computer to log a job.
S0.do: Keeps saving monthly on top of about ten months of bills already put aside. Keeps going to union branch meetings and keeps using the paper job form instead of the AI report tool for as long as she's allowed.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like watching a forecast storm blow out to sea.
S0.quote: I’m not proud of that, but I’d rather spend my energy up the pole than poking at a screen.
S0.fieldNote: Jade's relief is about being left alone more than about money, which is already secure. Her resistance to new tools is practical and a bit stubborn, and she admits a colleague quietly covers for it. She frames everything through the union contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly what the union is for. If tasks are going to machines, we bargain over it, who gets retrained, who keeps the overtime, what the robots are allowed to touch. I'd be loud about it at branch meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm mostly fine. They'll put drones on the inspection side and AI on the planning desk, and maybe some of the dispatchers go. But a pole on a back lane with a dog barking and a wasp nest in the transformer box, nobody's sending a robot up that soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every meeting where they talk about the new kit, and I'd push for a written agreement that no crew gets cut to three because a drone did the survey. I'd keep saving. I'd probably let them show me the drone stuff, because that's coming either way, but I wouldn't volunteer to be first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for me, more for the young ones on apprentice pay. It's that feeling of the ground shifting a little under the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran, our apprentice. He's twenty and he's good, but if they decide they need fewer new starters because the machines do the survey and the planning, he's the one they don't keep on. I'd be fighting for him before I'd be fighting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're mostly fine, but you'd still be pushing hard at meetings. Why both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because fine for me isn't the same as fine. My mum was a cleaner at the hospital when they outsourced it, and she kept her job, but everyone after her got worse terms. I watched that. I'm not letting it happen on my watch.

S1.say: I'd say this is exactly what the union is for, and that we have to bargain over which tasks machines take, who gets retrained and what the robots are allowed to touch.
S1.think: I think I'm mostly fine, because drones and planning software will take inspections and desk work long before a robot can climb a messy back-lane pole. The people at risk are dispatchers and young apprentices.
S1.do: Attends every meeting about new equipment and pushes for a written agreement that crews won't be cut to three because of drone surveys. Keeps saving, and agrees to be trained on drones without volunteering to go first.
S1.feel: Uneasy, less for herself than for apprentices on low pay, like the ground shifting slightly under the truck.
S1.quote: My mum was a cleaner at the hospital when they outsourced it, and she kept her job, but everyone after her got worse terms.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is for others, especially the apprentice Kieran, and it's rooted in watching her mother's workplace outsourced. Public and private views line up more than usual. She'd accept new kit if the union gets a say, but won't lead the way on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disaster, and that the government should have stopped the companies before it got this far. Online I'd be sharing every petition going. At work I'd be telling people to join the union now if they haven't, because that's the only door we'd have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think we'd be in real trouble. If a robot can do my work and Sam's work, because Sam's a nurse and they'd come for that too, then two years is nothing. Savings buy us about ten months. After that, I don't know what pays the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop every extra bit of spending the same week. The holiday we've booked for the summer, gone. I'd throw every spare pound at the mortgage while I still have the wage, and I'd be at the union office asking what the plan is, and writing to our MP, our member of parliament, every month. I wouldn't know what to retrain as, because what would be safe?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head. It'd feel like a fault you can't find, the whole street dark and no idea where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maisie's twelve, she'd read about it before I told her. I'd say Mum's still working for now and we've got money put by, which is true. Theo's nine, he'd just want to know if he can still do football, and I'd say yes, and then I'd go and cancel something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change compared to more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With two years there's no plan, there's only grabbing. The company would bring in the machines to save money before anyone's agreed what happens to us. Speed is what makes it cruel.

S2.say: I'd call it a disaster that government let companies push through, share every petition online, and tell everyone at work to join the union because it's the only door left.
S2.think: We'd be in real trouble, since both my job and my partner Sam's nursing job could go. Our savings cover about ten months, and after that I don't know what pays the mortgage.
S2.do: Cancels the family's summer holiday and cuts all extra spending in the first week. Puts every spare pound on the mortgage while the wage lasts, presses the union for a plan and writes to her member of parliament monthly.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over money, like hunting for a fault while the whole street is dark.
S2.quote: With two years there's no plan, there's only grabbing.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her calm breaks: two incomes at risk at once and no time to bargain. She can't name anything she'd retrain into, which fits her dislike of new tech. She blames the speed and the government's failure to restrain companies more than the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same line as before, but with a bit more fight. I'd say we've got five years to make the companies and the government sign something, a deal on wages or a fund for people who get pushed out. I'd be organising, not just complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but it's not enough for someone like me to become someone else. I'm forty-three. I'd be forty-eight when it lands, still with Theo at school and twelve years left on the mortgage. I'd be trying to get as far ahead as I could and hoping the union wins something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd overpay the mortgage hard, a few hundred a month extra, and keep the savings untouched. I'd stand for branch rep, which I've always said no to. Maybe I'd let them train me on the robot crews, if there's a job babysitting the machines, I'd take it over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be less stuck than with two years, because there'd be jobs to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for branch rep. What's stopped you before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, and I'm not a speaker. Gail does it now and she's brilliant. But if this was coming in five years, Gail can't carry it alone, and I'd rather be in the room than reading about it in an email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said you'd take a job looking after the machines. That's a change from refusing the report app.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I hear it. Pride's cheap when you're not scared. If it's that or nothing, I'll learn the screen. I'd still hate it, mind.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to make companies and government sign a deal, on wages or a fund for people pushed out, and I'd be organising rather than complaining.
S3.think: Five years helps, but I can't become someone else by forty-eight with a child at school and twelve years left on the mortgage. I'd get as far ahead as I can and hope the union wins something.
S3.do: Overpays the mortgage by a few hundred a month and leaves savings untouched. Stands for union branch rep for the first time, and would accept training to supervise robot crews rather than end up with nothing.
S3.feel: Anxious but busy, less stuck than with two years because there would be things to do.
S3.quote: Pride's cheap when you're not scared. If it's that or nothing, I'll learn the screen.
S3.fieldNote: When gently challenged on the contradiction with her refusal of the report app, she owned it straight away. The extra time turns her from protester into organiser. She still sees retraining as a last resort rather than a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. That's time to write the rules properly: who owns the robots, how the savings get shared, what happens to people like us. I'd be saying that at work and anywhere else I'm asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years might be worse in a way. Ten years of waiting for the axe. I'd be fifty-three when it lands, too young to stop and too old to start fresh. But I'd have the mortgage nearly done, which matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job, keep saving, and aim to clear the mortgage by fifty. I'd do the union rep thing properly. I'd probably think about the kids differently, steer Maisie away from anything a machine could do, though I've no idea what that would be by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a slow kind. Like a dentist appointment that's ten years away but you can't stop thinking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change for Maisie and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maisie wants to be a vet. I'd have said yes before, now I'd be wondering. I'd want her to do something with people, something you'd want a person for, like Sam does. But I'd be guessing, and I hate guessing about my kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three when it lands. What does that age mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad got laid off from the bus garage at fifty-four. He never worked properly again and he got bitter. I don't want to be him. I'd rather have the house paid off and fight from there.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift we shouldn't waste, and use it to write proper rules about who owns the robots and how the savings get shared with workers.
S4.think: Ten years could feel worse, like a long wait for the axe, and I'd be fifty-three, too young to stop and too old to start fresh. At least the mortgage would be nearly paid.
S4.do: Carries on working and saving with a target of clearing the mortgage by fifty. Takes the union rep role seriously, and starts rethinking her daughter's plans to study to be a vet.
S4.feel: A slow, steady anxiety, like a dentist appointment ten years off that she can't stop thinking about.
S4.quote: My dad got laid off from the bus garage at fifty-four. He never worked properly again and he got bitter.
S4.fieldNote: The longer runway doesn't calm her much, because her fear is tied to her father's late-career layoff. Paying off the house becomes her anchor. She's unsure about her children's futures and says so plainly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. What would help is a guarantee, in law, that if a company replaces crews with machines, part of that saving goes to the people it pushed out, for years, not a one-off cheque. And a say for unions on when the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who fixes the robots when they break in a storm at three in the morning. I'd like to know. Because right now that's me, and I'd want somebody to have thought about it.

headlineQuote: You didn't ask who fixes the robots when they break in a storm at three in the morning.
portrait: Jade Abbott is a 43-year-old overhead lineworker on a four-person bucket-truck crew in the city, married to Sam, a nurse, with two children and a mortgage on Harrow Road. She has about ten months of savings, a solid union contract and no interest in new tech, still writing job notes in a pocket book. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy but protective of apprentices under steady change. Fast AGI alarms her because both household incomes would be at risk with no time to bargain, while slower versions push her from protester into union organiser, focused on paying off the house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both her job and her partner's could go before anyone has a plan.
whatWouldHelp: A legal guarantee that companies replacing crews with machines share the savings with displaced workers for years, plus a union say over when robots come in.
